questions.q: How does this lesson's stakeholder work differ from the stakeholder identification in Lesson 2?
options: Lesson 2 covered external stakeholders only, and this lesson covers internal ones only
They are identical processes done twice for redundancy
Lesson 2 was a one-time broad pass to decide who needs a seat at the table; this lesson is narrower and ongoing, focused on who's affected by one specific change
This lesson replaces the need for Lesson 2 entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes the broad, one-time Chapter 1 pass from this lesson's narrower, change-specific, ongoing focus.

questions.q: What are the two axes used to map stakeholders in this lesson?
options: Department size and budget
Location and time zone
Influence (ability to block or accelerate the change) and impact (how much the change affects their daily work)
Seniority and tenure
questions.explain: The lesson defines the map using exactly these two axes: influence and impact.

questions.q: Per the lesson, what does the 'low influence, high impact' group need, and why is this group significant?
options: Executive-level one-on-one meetings
Only a general announcement, same as every other group
No attention at all, since they lack influence
Clear training and a visible channel to raise problems — it's usually the largest group, the people who actually have to use the new process
questions.explain: The lesson calls out this quadrant as usually the largest group, needing training and a way to flag problems even though no individual can block the rollout.

questions.q: What mistake does the lesson say most governance leads make with stakeholder communication?
options: Never communicating with stakeholders at all
Only communicating with the highest-influence group
Treating every stakeholder the same way with one generic announcement, which underserves both the highest-influence and highest-impact groups
Spending too much individual time with low-impact stakeholders
questions.explain: The lesson identifies a single generic announcement for everyone as the common mistake, since it fails to address differing needs by quadrant.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a stakeholder map needs to be revisited periodically?
options: Stakeholder maps are only valid for exactly one week
People change roles, previously quiet people can gain real influence, and champions can move to other departments
The map format itself expires and must be redrawn
Regulations require a new map every month
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a map drawn once at the start of a rollout goes stale as circumstances and people change.
